prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow optical frequency standards of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I move my preferred configuration from B018 to B040, a single prize part for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The chair asks whether my preference for IceCube rests chiefly on its being a new observational channel. It does, and I still think that is the most attractive kind of prize: nature supplied a clue we did not predict. But when I weigh B018 against the objections I wrote myself in round 1, they are the same objections my colleagues press, and they have not gone away. The dominant sources of the diffuse flux are unidentified, the source associations are statistically limited, KM3NeT and Baikal confirmation is still developing, and a two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND set aside, is something I cannot defend from the supplied evidence. B040 does not carry those problems. The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, original idea with a clear statement: it removes the trap-induced light shift on the clock transition so that thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once, and the platform has been taken to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and reproduced and compared across independent laboratories. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist. What changed my mind is the distinctness argument, which was my main hesitation. Kroll, Olsson, Pearce and Lindroth have stated it in terms I can accept: the comb of 2005 is a ruler for counting optical frequencies and the 2012 prize honoured control of individual quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, many-atom interrogation without a systematic shift, and rests on a different physical idea. It is not the whole of the precision-measurement lineage, but I judge it a distinct step rather than a third award for the same thing. I also accept that I did not rank B040 at all in my opening, which was a gap in my own assessment, not a finding about the clock.
statement.case_against: My reservation about distinctness is reduced but not removed. A critic can still say that Ye's own earlier comb work, the 2005 prize and the 2012 ion-clock lineage make this a third award in one measurement tradition, and the citation must carry the burden of showing otherwise by naming the magic-wavelength condition and the neutral-atom ensemble explicitly. Part of the claimed impact, the redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy, is still prospective, so the citation should rest on the demonstrated invention and the independently reproduced accuracy and not on those applications. A two-name credit also sets aside Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and I cannot verify from the supplied evidence the first successful lattice-clock operation or who led it. Finally, I am a theorist in gravity and cosmology, not an atomic physicist, and I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for judgments about precision-spectroscopy priority. If B040 stalls, I would want the committee to take B018 seriously again, restricted to the diffuse flux with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND acknowledged, and I would not regard it as a prize that has to wait for source astronomy.

responses.point: Kroll weights advances in what can be measured and how accurately, judges B040 distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes, would word the citation species-neutrally, and divides the credit by roles between Katori's concept and Ye's development.
responses.response: In round 1 I argued that this was a third step in one measurement lineage, and I asked you in effect to explain why. Your reply, that the comb supplied the ruler, the ion work showed control of one particle, and the lattice clock's contribution is the magic-wavelength condition that makes a large neutral ensemble usable, answers my objection well enough that I now accept it. I agree with your wording for the citation: name the invention and development of the lattice clock, not a record figure and not one species, since strontium and ytterbium both realise it. I also agree that a third name needs an argument from the supplied evidence and that none has been offered, so I support the pair. I note your Hall connection. It is a stay in Boulder, not a tie to Katori or Ye, and I do not think it calls for recusal, though I would let the committee record the disclosure.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved B040 to first, ranks IceCube as an alternative, and says the distinction rests on a conceptual step, the magic wavelength, and not on the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: You are right that my preference for B018 rests on the new-channel argument, and I accept your point that a measured flux whose astrophysical origin is open is a less settled result than one already reproduced at the 1e-18 level in several laboratories. Your attribution point also lands: a pair for IceCube leaves out the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage and does not represent the collaboration. Where I part from you, mildly, is that I do not think the unresolved sources make the diffuse-flux discovery premature in the way 2002 honoured detection before a completed neutrino astronomy. I would keep B018 first among my alternatives for a later year. For this year I agree with you that the clock is the better-defended prize, and I would not rest it on the redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Olsson asked why I left B040 off my opening ballot, said that if the reason is overlap with 2005 and 2012 she would want to answer it, and described the lattice clock as a new principle rather than a refinement, with the comb used as a tool.
responses.response: Your question was fair, and the answer is overlap, which I did not argue as carefully as I should have, together with the fact that I was thinking in terms of discoveries in nature and gave too little weight to inventions that change what can be measured. Your answer, that the comb is a tool every optical clock uses and the prize would not claim its invention, is the distinction I needed. I would add that the citation should say what the lattice contributes, a neutral-atom ensemble at a magic wavelength interrogated at optical frequency, so that the sentence itself answers the 2005 and 2012 objection. I also take your point about dividing the credit by roles. I would settle the first successful lattice-clock demonstration and its uncertainty budget from the record, before the citation speaks of who carried it out.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B040 first as a single coherent story, grants that I had a reason to ask about distinctness, and told me that B023 needs a clear statement of what is rewarded when five names are reduced to three.
responses.response: I agree with your assessment of B023, and it is part of why I withdrew from it in round 1 and no longer think the attribution problem can be solved. With COBE honoured in 2006, and Puget and Sunyaev outside any three-name list, the committee would be explaining its omissions more than its choice. On the clock, I take your answer that the 2005 citation covers a spectroscopic tool whereas this would reward a new kind of atomic clock with a different operating principle, and I note that you describe it as a judgement the committee should make explicitly. I make it: I accept the clock as distinct. I also accept your record that Katori's idea and Ye's accuracy work are the two threads later strontium and ytterbium clocks follow, and that Lemonde should be recorded without changing the pair.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the citation should be worded around the invention and development of the clock, not the record numbers, and that if prize-history overlap were disqualifying it would hurt B061 more than B040.
responses.response: I agree on the wording, since other groups continue to improve the numbers and a citation tied to a figure ages badly. I also accept your argument about overlap. Applying the same test to B061, adjacent to the 2016 prize in the same subject and missing Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang, I find it harder to defend than the clock, and I list it only as a fallback. Where I would qualify you is on the 2022 prize and B010. I am not as sure as you that QKD is only protocol-level, but I do not think the committee has the support to make it a second part, and I would not add one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, and I myself, can accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes once the citation states the magic-wavelength condition, which I now do but without full confidence.

Whether a two-name credit is sufficient given Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and what the first successful lattice-clock demonstration was; the supplied evidence does not settle it.
Whether the redefinition of the second should affect the timing of the prize, which I regard as an application and not a doubt about the invention, but which is still partly prospective.

Whether B018 would be mature enough in a later year, with source identification firmer and KM3NeT and Baikal confirming the diffuse flux, and how the credit could then represent AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND and the IceCube collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B040, B018 or B061. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) are not among the credited names. I work in theoretical cosmology and gravity, adjacent to B023 and B038, and I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the clock community. I have no documented link to Kroll's Boulder stay, and I do not see a recusal reason in his disclosure; I defer to the committee on that.
